sections.heading: Thanking you for carrying my sin
sections.text: Lord Jesus, my Savior, thank you with everything in me for your grace and love. You did not stand far off from my guilt. You carried my sin in your own body on the cross, and you did it for me. Help me not to treat that lightly. Let the wonder of your sacrifice keep reaching the deepest places in me.
theological_themes: Christ bore the believer’s sin personally and substitutionally on the cross.
Grace and love are seen most clearly in the self-giving of Christ.
Thanksgiving flows from knowing that salvation is not earned but received.

scripture_references.connection: Peter speaks of Christ bearing sins in his body on the tree, so this directly grounds the prayer’s gratitude for Jesus taking the sinner’s guilt upon himself at the cross.
Paul describes the Son of God as loving him and giving himself for him, which supports the personal tone of receiving Christ’s cross not merely as an idea but as mercy given to me.

sections.heading: Letting the cross reshape how I see everything
sections.text: Let your cross become the place I keep coming back to. When life tastes bitter, make it like the wood at Marah that made the water drinkable. Where things in me feel dead and barren, let your cross bring life and beauty, like the staff that budded. When I am helpless and wounded by sin, teach me to look to you in faith, like Israel looked at the serpent lifted up in the wilderness. Keep turning my eyes away from myself and toward you.
theological_themes: The cross changes how suffering, barrenness, guilt, and helplessness are understood before God.
Biblical images of Marah, the budding staff, and the lifted serpent express God bringing healing, life, and faith through what he appoints.
Faith looks away from self-rescue and toward God’s provided salvation.

scripture_references.connection: At Marah, God used a piece of wood to make bitter water sweet, which illuminates the prayer’s request that Christ’s cross transform bitter experiences into places of grace.

Israel’s healing came by looking at the lifted bronze serpent, an act of trusting God’s appointed remedy rather than their own strength; this supports the prayer’s plea for a faith-filled look to Christ.
Jesus himself connects the lifted serpent to his own lifting up, showing that the cross is the place where helpless sinners look to him and receive life.

sections.heading: Making the cross the center of my life with you
sections.text: By your cross, put my sins to death. Use it to draw me nearer to you. Make it the solid ground under my comfort, the energy behind my obedience, the heart of every promise you give in the gospel, and the help I cling to in trouble. Let it strengthen my love, deepen my gratitude, and grow every grace you are forming in me. Make the cross not a small part of my faith, but the center of it. And give me the kind of rest that is never lazy or cold—a settled rest that keeps overflowing in praise.
theological_themes: The cross is not only the basis of forgiveness but also the power and pattern of sanctification.
Union with Christ in his death means sin’s rule is broken and obedience becomes possible.
Christian comfort, gratitude, love, and worship are grounded in Christ crucified.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that believers are united with Christ in his death so that sin’s dominion is broken; this supports the request that the cross crucify sin and shape a new life for God.
Paul’s only boast is the cross of Christ, through which the world is crucified to him and he to the world; this grounds the prayer’s desire for the cross to become the center and substance of faith.
Paul says comfort overflows through Christ even in affliction, which supports asking that the cross become the believer’s comfort in trouble rather than merely a past event.

sections.heading: Accepting the cross you call me to carry
sections.text: Lord Jesus, you have also called me to take up a cross of my own before I receive the crown. You know exactly what obedience will cost me. You know the burdens, losses, humblings, and self-denials that belong to my path. My selfishness hates this. My flesh keeps arguing with you about it. I cannot carry it rightly, walk with it faithfully, or learn from it fruitfully unless you give me patient grace.
theological_themes: Discipleship includes self-denial, suffering, and obedience before glory.
The believer’s resistance to costly obedience exposes remaining sin and self-love.
Patience under the cross is not natural strength but grace received from Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus calls anyone who would follow him to deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow; this directly grounds the prayer’s acceptance of a personal cross in discipleship.
Paul links sharing in Christ’s sufferings with sharing in his glory, which supports the prayer’s movement from bearing the cross now toward receiving the crown later.
James speaks of steadfastness under trial and the promised crown of life, illuminating the prayer’s plea for patient endurance before final reward.

sections.heading: Receiving your grace with the burden
sections.text: Teach me to see that the cross you give is not cruel, even when it is hard. My rebellious will calls it hateful, and the load feels heavier when I keep trying to dodge it. Show me the mercy hidden in what you wisely allow. Remind me that you never send a cross without the grace you promise for it. Make me willing to carry what you place on me, patiently and closely with you, trusting that your yoke is easy and your burden is light because you are carrying me as I carry it.
theological_themes: God gives sustaining grace for the burdens he calls his people to bear.
The hardship of discipleship is transformed by fellowship with Christ and submission to his will.
Christ’s yoke is not weightless, but it is gracious, because he is gentle and sufficient for those who come to him.

scripture_references.connection: The Lord tells Paul that his grace is sufficient and his power is made perfect in weakness, which supports the prayer’s confidence that grace comes with the burden.

Jesus invites the weary to come to him and describes his yoke as easy and his burden as light; this directly grounds the prayer’s final trust that the cross carried with Christ is sustained by Christ.
Hebrews calls believers to endurance by looking to Jesus, who endured the cross before entering joy; this supports carrying one’s appointed path patiently with eyes fixed on him.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses several Old Testament images typologically: Marah’s sweetened waters, Aaron’s budding rod, and the bronze serpent. The bronze serpent has an explicit New Testament connection to Christ in John 3; the other images were retained as biblical metaphors for God bringing sweetness and life rather than asserted as formal prophecies of the cross.

The language of an appointed personal cross can be pastorally sensitive, especially for those enduring severe suffering or abuse. The adaptation preserves the doctrine of God’s providence and Christ’s call to costly discipleship while avoiding any suggestion that a person must passively remain in harm or that every suffering should be simplistically interpreted.

The original’s phrase “rest without rest” is paradoxical and could be misunderstood. It was rendered as settled rest that overflows in ongoing praise, preserving the idea of peace that is active rather than idle.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Carnal reason” was rendered as the flesh arguing with God, to preserve the original contrast between faith-shaped obedience and the natural mind’s resistance to costly discipleship.

“The very essence of my religion” was rendered as the cross being the center of faith, since in contemporary speech “religion” can sound merely institutional or external, while the original means the heart of lived Christianity.

“With my cross thou sendest promised grace” was interpreted as God giving sustaining grace for whatever obedience and suffering Christ calls the believer to bear, grounded especially in 2 Corinthians 12:9 and Matthew 11:28-30.
